CONVENTION TO COINCIDE WITH
PI ANNIVERSARY
PI
CHAPTER will be host to the 113th
annual convention of Psi Upsilon at Sy
racuse
University, June 22-23-24.
In assuming the position of host for the
first time since 1925, the Pi is anticipating
one of the largest turnouts of brethren in
fraternity history. This well-founded hope
is based on the fact that the Pi will cele
brate its 75th anniversary in conjunction
with the convention.
The heavy concentration of Pi men and
other chapter representation in upstate
New York is expected to produce a banner
attendance.
The eye-catching Pi chapter house, on
its imposing site overlooking the main
Syracuse University campus, will be the
center of convention activities and will
house approximately 30 of the ofiBcial dele
gates. Plans for housing of other delegates
are being developed by the committee and
call for location close to the chapter house.
Peter A. GaBauer, Pi '25, of New York
City is general chairman of "combined
operations" for the convention and anni
versary celebration, with Joseph L. Hue
ber, Pi '24, of Syracuse as co-chairman.
Dr. George S. Reed, Pi '08, is general
chairman of the Pi's 75th festivities with
Maxwell L. Scott, Pi '28, New York City,
as co-chairman.
The committees working on the ap
proaching convention aim to make the
annual banquet at the Hotel Syracuse a
"memorable occasion," to quote Chairman
GaBauer. On the lighter side, the program
will be climaxed with a clambake Satur
day afternoon and evening, June 24, at
the nearby Skaneateles Country Club.

THIS

�a

spirit of the West, as the blaze of autumn
glory on the hills of central New York,
where the story unfolds. . . .
The state convention of the Methodist
Episcopal Church of New York, meeting
in Syracuse, approved a
plan to establish
a
University and in cooperation with the
city fathers founded Syracuse University
on
February 22, 1870. Its first Board of
Trustees envisioned a
great university
which, in character and philosophy, would
exemplify the American traditions of
equality and freedom. It would offer edu
cation to all youth. Its curriculum would
be rich in the disciplines of knowledge . . .
an education for life, not just livelihood.
The first Board of Trustees wisely agreed
that the first college in this program of a
liberal education should be the College of
Liberal Arts. It was established as the
foundation upon which the structure would
depend. The first degrees granted were
Liberal Arts degrees, and the first building
on the campus was the Hall of Languages,
still the home of that College and the
symbol of the University.
It is indicative of the spirit of that first
board that the first expansion of the new
university was in the training of physicians.
The faculty of the medical department of
Geneva College proposed to the trustees
of Syracuse University that their depart
ment be moved to Syracuse for the greater
opportunity of medical education. Their

1872.

the founders next sought expansion in the

BUD WILKINSON EARNS AWARD AS
COACH OF YEAR
By Mackabness H. Goode, Xi '35
yOU'VE
read about the Oklahoma
Sooners' meteoric rise to top rank in
U. S. football. Bud Wilkinson, Mu '37, is
two of the three reasons for their success.
"On the first play of the fourth period,
Mel Lyle ran an end-around for Louisiana
State, and we have never seen it run more
ferociously. And we've never seen a
foot
ball agent greeted more
robustly. A shoetop tackle lifted Lyle into the air where
he was almost torn in two by a following
thunderbolt. He lost the ball, hut was
fortunate in retaining his head. . . . Yet
the game was
played with excessive clean
liness. It was
simply man-sized. . . ."
Thus a bemused Memphis sportswriter
tried to sum
up the Sugar Bowl game that
climaxed the greatest season that Okla
homa University had had in 30 years.
It was no fluke that Oklahoma came into
the Sugar Bowl with a
winning streak of
20 successive games behind them. From
the day that Brother Bud Wilkinson, Mu
'37, stepped into the head coach's job back
in 1947, the Sooners began to show a class
they hadn't shown in ten years. By 1948
they were on their way to winning 26 out
of 27 games and a
ranking, with Notre
Dame, as one of the two top teams in the
country. If you read the sports pages this
winter, you aheady know that Brother
Wilkinson, at the age of 34, was voted
Coach of the Year by the American Foot
ball Coaches Association by a
plurality
that would not have disappointed a Demo
cratic political candidate in Gulfport, Mis
sissippi. Ex-President Hoover was the prin
cipal speaker when the award was
pre
sented. (See frontispiece.)
You may also know that the U. S. Junior
Chamber of Commerce recently named
Bud one of the 10 outstanding young men
of 1949.
If you don't know the University of
Oklahoma, however, you may wonder just
how much these honors prove about a

ings when he challenged Bud to see what

That brings us
right back to our
original
questions. What about the additions to the

of a
championship team? Which comes
first these days�the stadium or the quar
terback? Is one a
capital investment and the
other an
operating expense? In Oklahoma's
case the record shows that growth in facili
ties and in the support of the team have
gone together in a natural and healthy way
with the increasing success of Brother
Wilkinson's squad.
It is true that Dr. George L. Cross,
president of the university, is proud of the
team and proud of the fact that O.U. now
attracts over 50,000 people to its games.
It is true that spectators and players are
comfortably cared for. It is also true that
the university's athletic department does
an effective job of stimulating interest in
sports. Athletic-minded youngsters are be
ing attracted to the university.
But, and here is where Brother Wilkin
son's team makes such a
pleasing contrast
with many of the top teams of recent
years, the players are drawn from the
University's natural sphere of influence�
the state of Oklahoma. Coal miners, steel
workers, and stevedores do not arrive in
small muscle-bound groups in August and
quietly depart in November. The names
and home towns shown on O.U. football
programs read with refreshing simpHcity
�George Thomas^ from Fairland, Lindell
Pearson and Jim Owens from Oklahoma
City, Stanley West from Enid, Darrell
Royal and Leon Heath from HoUis and so
on. The list sounds like the people in a
back-yard soft-ball game.
And one other point ought not to be
overlooked in this connection. You prob
ably remember the sad case of the coach
with his back to the wall. Injury after in
jury had riddled his squad. Finally, one
of his already damaged players was car
ried off, done for the day. "And now what
do I do?" the coach cried. "Put in a stu
dent?" Bud Wilkinson's teams are made up
of students. Eighteen members of the
squad graduate this year, and all but one,
a
physical education major, are taking
straight academic courses.
So, the first element in Bud's success has
been an
adequate supply of non-profes
sional players in a school that likes foot
ball.
The next element brings us around to
Bud himself. Comments on his team's play
all point back to the kind of coach he is.
Someone has called the Oklahoma 1949
team "a football squad with a furious en
joyment of down-field blocking." A Denver
sportswriter says that Oklahoma had the
fastest charging line he had ever seen.
Arch Ward of the Chicago Tribune
summed up by comparing Bud with Frank
Leahy of Notre Dame�"Both are
perfec
tionists. . . . Both are tireless workers. . . .
Both have teams whose daring play re
flects the imagination of their leaders. . . .
Both also are
great gentlemen. . . ."
Bud's own background as a
player, of
course, is tops. By the time he joined the
Mu in 1933 he had already been captain
of the Shattuck Military Academy team at
Faribault. In his sophomore year he won
a
place for himself on Minnesota's unde
feated national championship team as a
running guard. In the following year, on
another one of Bernie Bierman's national
championship teams, he was so
good that
Grantland Rice called him "one of the
greatest running guards of all time." He
completed his final season, on a third na
tional championship team, as
quarterback.
Active in the Mu chapter�"always ready
for Psi U songfests"�Bud found time to

74 THE DIAMOND OF PSI UPSILON
make All American as
goalie in his third
year on the Minnesota hockey team. When
he added two years on the golf team and
steady "B" work in the classroom, it was
only natural that he should receive the
Western Conference medal for "outstand
ing proficiency in scholarship and athletics."
Just to show that he had something left
after this active undergraduate career. Bud
quarterbacked the College All Stars in
1937 to a
victory over the Green Bay
Packers�the first time in history that an
amateur team had ever beaten a
profes
sional one.
From there he went to Syracuse for an
M.A. in Enghsh, staying on until 1941 as
golf and hockey coach as well as assistant
to head football coach, Ossie Solem. His
Navy time was divided between sea
duty
on the air-craft carrier Enterprise and as
sisting in coaching the Iowa Pre-Flight
School's undefeated Sea Hawks.
When you count in other time assisting
at Minnesota and Oklahoma, you can see
that Bud was well grounded indeed when
he took over the head coach's whistle in
1947. He had outstanding experience as a
player and a
good deal of time behind him
as an assistant coach.
But one other factor was needed to
make the Sooners the outstanding team
that they were. There could have been
plenty of good material driven by a hard
working coach and still without this third
element the team might never have set
any prairies on fire. In Bud's case, as with
most top-flight coaches, it just happens
that he is also a first-rate creative strate
gist.
Starting with the split-T offense orig
inated by Don Faurot of the University
of Missouri, Bud has worked out an of
fense that introduces a
completely new
conception of what you can ask linemen
and backs to do in the course of a football
game.
One of Bud's theories is that if your en
tire forward wall outcharges the opposi
tion, your quarterback can run
laterally
down the line of scrimmag.3. Notice we
say down the line of scrimmage, not "be
hind" it. If you can convince your players
it's possible, this maneuver has a
couple of
immediate advantages. Even if a
play is
an
abject failure, the quarterback, who
handles the ball on most plays, loses no
ground; he's stopped on the line of scrim
mage. And if the running, back receives
the ball as
planned, he is over the line a
fraction of a second later. To make his
linemen as effective as
possible. Bud spaces
them at unorthodox intervals and en
courages them to shift away from these
positions, too, ff they believe new loca
tions will further harass and depress the
opposition.
If a Sooner lineman is called on to do
things over and above the normal call of
duty, the backs are not allowed to coast,
either. Starting closeup in a combination
of a
split-T formation with a
wing back
thrown in for good measure, the backfield
goes off like a
pinwhsel spitting fire in
half a dozen directions. In most of the
plays the back carrying the ball never even
has a chance to see what he's handling.
The ball is placed on his outside hip and
the back keeps his eyes on the road with
out stopping to ask questions. After all,
the success of an offensive play is only
measured by the distance the ball goes
forward.
This is a
sample of the kind of thinking
Bud Wilkinson brings to his profession.
Oklahoma, playing in the big Seven, had
had only one really good year since 1920
until Bud Wilkinson started to operate.
Last year they were so
good that they
were
compared over and over
again with
Notie Dame, the team you always have to
beat if you want clear title to top rank in
the country. No conclusion could be
reached because the two teams were not
on each other's schedules.
Ill this spring, Bud will be starting all
over in the fall again with only one man
back from his first team. But we have a
clue to his thinking for the future: Notre
Dame comes on to the regular Oklahoma
schedule starting in '52.

THE ARCHIVES
By Henry C.
Early Presidents of
OUR
noble old Fraternity during its
first years gained stature "without
dependence on
any central administrative
or executive body." It was bound to hap
pen, however, so at the Convention held
with the Gamma in 1857, an Executive
Committee of three was elected, who with
successors, carried on until the Constitu
tion of 1869 (Convention with the Theta)
created the Executive Council as it has
been in existence ever since.
First president of the Executive Coun
cil was Wilham Forbes Morgan, Delta '65,
who served 1869-1874. His picture, oppo
site page 644 of the Annals of Psi Upsilon,
clearly reveals why under him "the Execu
tive Council made a
beginning which
merited and won the approval and trust
